title: Differentiable Schwarz-Coupled Solvers for Thin Boundary Layer Transport: Inverse Modeling via Agentic AI Optimization
authors: Siva Viknesh, Amirhossein Arzani
abstract: High-Péclet-number transport problems give rise to thin boundary layers with steep near-wall gradients whose accurate solution requires high-resolution meshes and could challenge inverse modeling. To address this challenge, we develop an overlapping Schwarz domain-decomposition framework grounded in perturbation theory, in which an inner equation governs near-wall dynamics and an outer equation governs bulk transport, and both subproblems are discretized using the finite element method and assembled into a fully differentiable multidomain physics solver. The formulation permits coarser mesh resolutions, reducing computational cost relative to a single-domain formulation. Exploiting the differentiability of the coupled solver, we formulate inverse problems in which the governing equations and boundary conditions are imposed as hard constraints, with the Schwarz coupling enforcing interface continuity. To accelerate the resulting adjoint-based optimization, we integrate large language models (LLMs) into the inverse workflow in two distinct configurations: a standalone optimizer that proposes successive parameter updates from the adjoint-computed sensitivities and an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) approach with access to the complete solver workflow, enabling it to perform multistage optimization procedures. The agentic AI configuration is shown to be most advantageous when the spatially varying unknown is represented in a functional basis rather than a high-dimensional nodal field representation. In this case, the AI agent grows the library of candidate basis functions during optimization under a prescribed admission policy, admitting predefined families in stages and initializing their parameters. In short, our proposed framework integrates Schwarz-coupled differentiable physics with agentic AI optimization for the inverse modeling of multiscale transport problems.

infographic.key_insight: A differentiable Schwarz-coupled finite element solver combines near-wall and bulk transport models to support inverse modeling of thin boundary layers with coarser meshes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could reduce computational cost when identifying unknown parameters in high-Péclet transport problems with steep near-wall gradients.
method: Split near-wall and bulk dynamics using perturbation theory and overlapping Schwarz domain decomposition.
Differentiate through coupled FEM solves, enforcing governing equations, boundary conditions, and interface continuity.
Use adjoint sensitivities with an LLM optimizer or a workflow-enabled AI agent that expands a functional basis under a prescribed admission policy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports lower computational cost than a single-domain formulation and greater agentic AI benefit for functional-basis unknowns than for high-dimensional nodal fields, but provides no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance may depend on overlap design, mesh resolution, and the basis-admission policy; quantitative accuracy and speedup evidence is needed.
infographic.paper_title: Differentiable Schwarz-Coupled Solvers for Thin Boundary Layer Transport: Inverse Modeling via Agentic AI Optimization

title: Finite Element Modeling of Fracture in Brittle Foods with Physically Consistent Parameter Calibration: A Practical Case Study on Cooled Dark Chocolate
authors: Patrick Kurzeja, Felix Rörentrop, Kai Langenfeld, Jörn Mosler
abstract: Fracture in food can be undesired during production and transportation but also intended during cutting, grinding or mastication. The associated peak load, the deformation at failure and the resulting fragment geometry are all product properties. This work condenses the modeling of such fracture into a physically rigorous recipe that considers the practical constraints imposed by finite element simulations where necessary and applies idealized theoretical assessments where applicable. Cooled dark chocolate serves as a reproducible model material. Two well-established modeling frameworks for Griffith-type brittle fracture are assessed at an affordable spatial discretization: a sharp-interface and a diffuse phase-field approach. The assessment covers the choice of numerical framework, its discretization and a staged identification of the model parameters. Each parameter is identified from the loading stage that governs it: elastic parameters from pre-crack tension and compression, critical energy release rate from three-point-bending peak force, and the phase-field width last. The phase-field width interferes with the structural response, crack curvature and stress fields, depending on its lower bound set by the affordable spatial resolution. Elastic slope, peak force and crack path therefore cannot be met practically by a single parameter set. The objective must be fixed for the calibration of the model parameters and reported together with the numerical parameters and the boundary value problem.

infographic.key_insight: At affordable mesh resolution, brittle-fracture models for cooled dark chocolate cannot practically match elastic slope, peak force and crack path with a single parameter set, so calibration must prioritize a stated objective.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Objective-specific fracture calibration can support simulations of food breakage during production, transport, cutting and mastication.
method: Compare sharp-interface and diffuse phase-field frameworks for Griffith-type brittle fracture.
Identify elastic parameters from pre-crack tension and compression, then critical energy release rate from three-point-bending peak force.
Calibrate phase-field width last and report the calibration objective, numerical parameters and boundary value problem.
infographic.evidence_signal: The assessment uses cooled dark chocolate as a reproducible model material and evaluates elastic response, bending peak force and crack behavior at affordable spatial discretization.
infographic.watch_item: Mesh resolution constrains the minimum phase-field width, which can alter structural response, crack curvature and stress fields.
infographic.paper_title: Finite Element Modeling of Fracture in Brittle Foods with Physically Consistent Parameter Calibration: A Practical Case Study on Cooled Dark Chocolate

title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity
authors: Yue Wu, Yuan Tian, Deng Pan, Mingwei Chen
abstract: Adapting a pre-trained machine-learning interatomic potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity requires improving defect accuracy without degrading the near-equilibrium elastic and vibrational response. Here we achieve this balance for the aluminium MACE potential QP17 by integrating conditional readout uncertainty, iterative full-parameter updates and protocol-compatible relative-energy anchoring. Sensitivities over 144 linear readout weights guide acquisition, with within-batch covariance updates and evolving neural representations. After four active-learning rounds (32 acquired configurations and 400 gradient updates), force-uncertainty acquisition reduces mean development force error from 22.43 to 21.52 meV/Angstrom, outperforming random sampling (22.70), geometry-diversity selection (22.46) and uniform training across all 104 candidate labels (22.71) under the same update budget. All three force-uncertainty runs satisfy bulk-mechanical retention criteria: historical relative-energy error decreases from 0.375 to 0.207 meV/atom, while harmonic phonon root-mean-square drift remains below 0.05 THz. Matched objective ablations reveal that relative-energy anchoring suppresses harmonic drift. Out-of-sample evaluations across planar faults, twin boundaries and grain boundaries demonstrate transferable gains in defect energies and deviatoric stresses, even though virial stresses are never fitted. A closed-loop molecular dynamics and density functional theory (MD-DFT) pilot confirms that automated acceptance gating intercepts updates that violate historical elastic-group energy or vibrational tolerances. Together, these components establish a retention-constrained fine-tuning protocol for improving plastic-deformation observables while preserving the tested bulk mechanical response.

infographic.key_insight: Uncertainty-guided, retention-constrained fine-tuning improves an aluminium MACE potential for defect dynamics while preserving tested bulk elastic and vibrational behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The protocol supports more reliable atomistic simulations of aluminium plasticity without sacrificing near-equilibrium mechanical fidelity.
method: Acquire configurations using uncertainty from sensitivities over 144 readout weights, updating covariance within each batch.
Iteratively fine-tune all model parameters with relative-energy anchoring to retain historical behavior.
Gate updates against historical elastic-group energy and vibrational tolerances.
infographic.evidence_signal: After four rounds, 32 acquired configurations and 400 gradient updates, mean development force error fell from 22.43 to 21.52 meV/Å, outperforming sampling baselines; all three force-uncertainty runs met retention criteria, with harmonic phonon RMS drift below 0.05 THz.
infographic.watch_item: Retention is demonstrated only for the tested aluminium potential and evaluation conditions; broader deployment requires renewed validation and acceptance gating.
infographic.paper_title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity

title: AI at a Turning Point: From ChatGPT through Neural Networks to Neuromorphic AI
authors: Volker Kempe
abstract: The tension between the established technologies of connectionist AI and their neuromorphic challengers is attracting growing attention, above all because of the enormous energy demand of the former and the low power consumption of the latter. Developing and running large AI models consumes gigawatt- to terawatt-hours of energy, while the human brain operates on a continuous 20 watts. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) counter this energy demand with a frugal approach and bring elements of self-organization into the methodological repertoire of AI: local learning instead of global error backpropagation, event-driven computing, and time as a carrier of information. They do not replace today's AI but extend it; in hybrid systems each approach can be deployed where its strengths lie. This monograph explains the field in a generally accessible yet mathematically rigorous way. Using the text-generation module of ChatGPT as an example, the principle, elegance, and computational cost of transformer-based AI are presented and compared with the coding, learning, and network-design methods of SNNs. Throughout, relevant mechanisms of the human nervous system serve as model and reference point. Topics include spike-timing-dependent plasticity, population and temporal coding, the Neural Engineering Framework, neuromorphic hardware from Loihi 2 to commercial edge processors, and the prospects for classical and neuromorphic AI to complement and extend each other.

infographic.key_insight: Spiking neural networks offer an event-driven, potentially energy-efficient complement to transformer-based AI rather than a wholesale replacement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Neuromorphic approaches may support low-power engineering sensing and edge inference, although the abstract reports no solid-mechanics application.
method: Explain transformer principles and computational costs using ChatGPT text generation.
Compare spiking-network coding, local learning, and network design with conventional AI.
Review neural mechanisms, the Neural Engineering Framework, and neuromorphic hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a comparative monograph, citing a roughly 20-watt human-brain reference but reporting no controlled benchmarks or measured model-to-model energy savings.
infographic.watch_item: Practical energy advantages require workload-specific evaluation that accounts for accuracy, hardware, and system overhead.
infographic.paper_title: AI at a Turning Point: From ChatGPT through Neural Networks to Neuromorphic AI

title: $H^2$-based equilibrated residual error estimates
authors: Kexin Ding, Yuwen Li
abstract: We develop a framework for equilibrated residual a posteriori error analysis of finite element methods, based on decomposing vector- and tensor-valued Sobolev spaces into $H^2$ and $H^1$ spaces. To estimate the residual functional acting on $H^2$ component, the method reconstructs symmetric and piecewise polynomial tensors on vertex patches in broken $H(\operatorname{div}\operatorname{div})$ spaces. We apply the proposed framework to conforming finite element discretizations of biharmonic equation, Poisson's equation, and linear elasticity in mixed form. As a result, we obtain several novel equilibrated residual a posteriori error estimates, providing guaranteed error control for energy error of biharmonic equation, $L^2$ norm error of Poisson's equation, and stress error of mixed linear elasticity. They also serve as the first polynomial-degree-robust a posteriori lower bounds of discretization errors. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of the $H^2$-based error estimators.

infographic.key_insight: An H²-based equilibrated residual framework provides guaranteed finite element error control and polynomial-degree-robust a posteriori lower bounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports reliable error assessment for plate bending, Poisson problems, and stress prediction in mixed linear elasticity.
method: Decompose vector- and tensor-valued Sobolev spaces into H² and H¹ components.
Reconstruct symmetric, piecewise-polynomial tensors on vertex patches in broken H(div div) spaces.
Derive equilibrated residual estimates for biharmonic energy error, Poisson L² error, and elasticity stress error.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments illustrate estimator effectiveness, but the abstract reports no quantitative accuracy or computational-cost results.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation requires specialized local tensor reconstructions; their computational overhead is not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: $H^2$-based equilibrated residual error estimates

title: Scaling of Interface Variability in Aerospace Composite Structures: A Multi-scale Stochastic Approach from Local Identification to Panel Response
authors: Elton Donfack-Siewe, Sylvain Dubreuil, Christian Fagiano, Jérôme Morio, Jean-Philippe Navarro
abstract: Quantifying random spatial variations in composite interface properties is an essential prerequisite for the high-fidelity propagation of material properties variabilities through structural numerical models. This study proposes a multi-scale stochastic framework designed to bridge the gap between local interfacial characterization at the coupon scale and the global response of industrial aerospace panels, focusing specifically on the skin-stringer bond line. Building upon previous stochastic modeling and identification methodologies for Mode I fracture, we first extend the likelihood-free Bayesian calibration to Mode II configurations to characterize interfacial stochastic parameters using experimental coupon data. To address the scale-up challenge, we employ a simulation-based Stochastic Finite Element Method (SFEM) to contrast two distinct probabilistic strategies -- spatially uniform variations (Paradigm 2) and spatially correlated random fields (Paradigm 3) -- against the traditional industrial B-basis standard (Paradigm 1). The numerical results reveal a dual mechanism in uncertainty propagation depending on the targeted airframe design criterion. For global performance, such as the ultimate load capacity, a significant scale effect leads to an uncertainty attenuation phenomenon; statistical averaging smooths out local heterogeneities, demonstrating that a computationally efficient spatially uniform approach is sufficient. Conversely, for local integrity, such as the threshold and spatial localization of early damage initiation, the inclusion of spatially correlated random fields becomes indispensable to capture premature degradation driven by local material weak spots. This balanced probabilistic treatment offers a route toward test derisking and predictive uncertainty management in the design of damage-tolerant aerospace composite airframes.

infographic.key_insight: Scale-driven averaging attenuates uncertainty in panel ultimate load, while spatially correlated interface variability remains essential for predicting early damage initiation and location.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Match uncertainty-model complexity to the design criterion: spatially uniform variability for global capacity and correlated random fields for local damage in aerospace skin–stringer bonds.
method: Extend likelihood-free Bayesian calibration from Mode I to Mode II using experimental coupon data.
Propagate interface variability from coupons to panels using simulation-based stochastic finite elements.
Compare industrial B-basis, spatially uniform variability, and spatially correlated random-field approaches.
infographic.evidence_signal: Coupon experiments support stochastic parameter identification, and panel simulations indicate uncertainty attenuation in ultimate load but sensitivity of early damage to local weak spots.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report quantitative accuracy or panel-scale experimental validation, so applicability beyond the studied configurations needs verification.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling of Interface Variability in Aerospace Composite Structures: A Multi-scale Stochastic Approach from Local Identification to Panel Response

title: Multiscale evaluation of the elastic response of polycrystalline NiAl using molecular statics, EBSD-based finite element and analytical homogenization methods
authors: Szymon Nosewicz, Marcin Maździarz, Paweł Hołobut, Witold Chromiński, Katarzyna Kowalczyk-Gajewska, Grzegorz Jurczak
abstract: The presented work proposes a multiscale framework for the numerical and analytical determination of the elastic constants of the intermetallic nickel aluminide (NiAl) at the microscopic scale. Molecular dynamics (MD) calculations have been employed to evaluate the stiffness tensors of a single NiAl monocrystalline body with cubic Pm$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The atomistic results were transferred to the upper scale as an input to micromechanical models. Here, finite element modeling (FEM) and analytical homogenization methods were used to simulate the elastic behavior of polycrystalline NiAl, with special attention to grain anisotropy and its morphology. The microstructural features of the heterogeneous body were evaluated experimentally using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and subsequently used to generate a 3D polycrystalline geometric model that preserves realistic distributions of grain orientations and grain sizes. The reconstructed NiAl polycrystal was subjected to uniaxial tensile test simulations using FEM to evaluate the effective Young's modulus ($E$) and Poisson's ratio ($ν$). The numerical results were confronted with the experimental values of $E$ and~$ν$. With these model assumptions, a very good agreement between numerical and experimental results was achieved. Finally, the experimental results were compared with classical analytical estimates. Among the analytical approaches, the Hashin-Shtrikman upper bound and self-consistent approximation reproduced the experimental Young's modulus with minor deviations.

infographic.key_insight: Atomistic stiffness calculations coupled with EBSD-informed finite elements accurately reproduced the elastic response of polycrystalline NiAl under the study’s modeling assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework links crystal-scale stiffness and realistic grain structure to effective elastic properties for engineering analysis of NiAl components.
method: Calculate the single-crystal NiAl stiffness tensor atomistically.
Build a 3D polycrystal using EBSD-derived grain orientation and size distributions.
Simulate uniaxial tension with FEM and compare effective properties with analytical homogenization estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports very good FEM–experiment agreement for Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio, with minor Young’s modulus deviations for the Hashin–Shtrikman upper bound and self-consistent approximation.
infographic.watch_item: No numerical errors are reported in the abstract, and accuracy depends on the atomistic inputs and reconstructed microstructure; no AI surrogate is described.
infographic.paper_title: Multiscale evaluation of the elastic response of polycrystalline NiAl using molecular statics, EBSD-based finite element and analytical homogenization methods

title: Evaluation of upper-scale mechanical parameters of particulate aluminum-based nanocomposites from molecular simulations
authors: Bartosz Bucholc, Marcin Maździarz, Szymon Nosewicz
abstract: This paper focuses on the numerical and analytical determination of the mechanical parameters of aluminum-matrix nanocomposites using atomistic-scale simulations within a multiscale modeling framework. Molecular statics simulations were employed to evaluate the tensile and compressive behavior of Al based composites reinforced with nanosized alumina particles. Two classes of atomistic models were investigated. First, a unit-cell model containing a single Al2O3 monocrystal embedded in an aluminum matrix was used to examine the influence of the volume fraction of the ceramic inclusion on the effective mechanical properties. Second, a polycrystalline RVE model comprising an alumina particle was analyzed to assess the effect of the number of Al grains on effective properties. For each case, the mechanical response was characterized by stress-strain curves, enabling the identification of upper-scale material parameters associated with the elastic regime (bulk, shear and Young's modulus) and the damage stage (ultimate strength, ultimate strain, and failure strain). The isotropized elastic constants evaluated from molecular simulations were compared with classical Voigt-Reuss-Hill bounds to assess their applicability in the elastic regime. Finally, atomistic-scale simulation outputs provided insight into the dominant deformation/damage mechanisms (brittle versus ductile) and fracture modes (transgranular versus intergranular).

infographic.key_insight: Atomistic simulations connect alumina reinforcement fraction and aluminum grain structure to effective elastic properties, strength, and failure behavior of aluminum-matrix nanocomposites.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports multiscale material modeling by extracting continuum-scale elastic and damage parameters from nanoscale mechanical responses.
method: Run molecular statics simulations under tension and compression.
Vary alumina volume fraction in single-inclusion unit cells and aluminum grain count in polycrystalline representative volume elements.
Extract elastic and failure parameters from stress–strain curves and compare isotropized elastic constants with Voigt–Reuss–Hill estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports stress–strain-based evaluation of moduli, ultimate strength, ultimate strain, and failure strain, alongside analysis of deformation and fracture mechanisms, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability to engineering loading conditions requires validation beyond the atomistic model sizes and molecular-statics conditions described.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluation of upper-scale mechanical parameters of particulate aluminum-based nanocomposites from molecular simulations

title: Unweaving the mechanics of woven fabrics through automated model discovery
authors: Marin Lauber, Uzair Manack, Thibault Vervenne, Rogier P. Krijnen, Benjamin Alheit, Nele Famaey
abstract: Woven fabrics have multiple structural, aesthetic, and medical applications that require knowledge of their mechanical properties. While isolated fiber properties are easily determined, bulk properties of woven material, which can be coated or locally reinforced, require knowledge of yarn density, weave style, and other characteristics that are difficult to obtain experimentally. Additionally, fiber rearrangement, twist, yarn contact, and fiber-direction coupling result in non-linear mechanical responses. As a result, there is no universal material model for woven materials, and each fabric requires a specific model and parameter calibration. Recently, methods to simultaneously discover material models and their parameters from experimental or synthetic datasets have been proposed. Here, we use automated model discovery to simultaneously extract the material model and its parameters from biaxial test data of a TPU-coated woven nylon fabric. We show that Constitutive Artificial Neural Networks discover a sparse three-term hyperelastic material law with one isotropic and two anisotropic contributions, reproducing the measured biaxial response with a mean $R^2=0.97$. Across 20 initializations, predictive accuracy remains robust despite variations in the exact sparse representation, consistent with strong correlations between several candidate terms. LARS-LASSO independently recovers the same dominant constitutive contributions at approximately 100-fold lower computational cost. These results are directly applicable to numerical finite-element models of fabric-based structures, including soft robotic devices. More broadly, these results provide a foundation for further model discovery, improved constitutive modeling, and mechanistically informed optimization of woven fabric structures.

infographic.key_insight: Automated model discovery identified a sparse three-term hyperelastic law for TPU-coated woven nylon, combining one isotropic and two anisotropic contributions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The discovered law can support finite-element simulations of fabric-based structures, including soft robotic devices.
method: Fit Constitutive Artificial Neural Networks to biaxial test data to discover model terms and parameters jointly.
Assess predictive robustness across 20 initializations.
Use LARS-LASSO to independently identify dominant constitutive contributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The neural-network-discovered models reproduced measured biaxial responses with mean R² = 0.97, while LARS-LASSO recovered the same dominant contributions at approximately 100-fold lower computational cost.
infographic.watch_item: Correlated candidate terms produced different sparse representations with similar accuracy, so the exact constitutive form may not be uniquely identifiable.
infographic.paper_title: Unweaving the mechanics of woven fabrics through automated model discovery

title: Higher-Order QMC Galerkin FEM for Singular Perturbation: Reaction-Diffusion with Affine-Parametric Reaction
authors: Fabian Rohner, Christoph Schwab
abstract: We analyze higher-order quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) Galerkin discretizations for a singularly perturbed reaction-diffusion problem with an affine-parametric reaction coefficient. We derive error estimates that are robust with respect to the perturbation parameter $\varepsilon$. To this end, we establish $\varepsilon$-uniform stability and mixed-parametric regularity estimates in an $\varepsilon$-weighted energy norm, with constants independent of the parameter dimension and of $\varepsilon$. These estimates imply robust dimension truncation estimates and dimension-independent higher-order QMC error bounds for linear quantities of interest. Assuming an abstract, $\varepsilon$-robust finite element approximation property, we combine the parametric estimates with the spatial discretization analysis to derive a general fully discrete QMC-FE error estimate with constants independent of both the parameter dimension and $\varepsilon$. We verify this approximation property for a one-dimensional model problem using continuous piecewise affine finite elements on Shishkin meshes. Numerical experiments illustrate the predicted robustness and convergence rates.

infographic.key_insight: Higher-order QMC–Galerkin finite element analysis yields error bounds independent of parameter dimension and the singular perturbation parameter ε.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports reliable uncertainty quantification for reaction–diffusion models with small ε, where sharp boundary layers challenge standard discretizations.
method: Establish ε-uniform stability and mixed-parametric regularity in an ε-weighted energy norm.
Combine dimension truncation and higher-order QMC integration with robust finite element approximation.
Verify the spatial approximation property in 1D using piecewise affine elements on Shishkin meshes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theoretical error estimates are complemented by numerical experiments illustrating the predicted robustness and convergence rates.
infographic.watch_item: The fully discrete guarantee assumes ε-robust spatial approximation, verified here only for a one-dimensional model problem.
infographic.paper_title: Higher-Order QMC Galerkin FEM for Singular Perturbation: Reaction-Diffusion with Affine-Parametric Reaction

title: A Differentiable, GPU-Accelerated Finite-Element Formulation in JAX for Large-Deformation Shells with Contact: Application to Patient-Specific Aortic Valve Simulation
authors: Mohsen Nakhaei, Alison M. Pouch, Matthew A. Jolley, Wensi Wu
abstract: Patient-specific aortic-valve models can help assess how tissue properties and geometry influence leaflet deformation and coaptation, with potential to inform intervention planning. Large deformations, near-incompressibility, and evolving contact make these simulations computationally demanding and can challenge nonlinear convergence. Differentiable, GPU-accelerated methods offer efficient derivative evaluation and parallel computation, but their matrix-free application to soft-tissue shells with contact remains less established. We developed a forward solver using tatva's energy-based finite-element framework in JAX. The solver combines finite-strain extensible-director shells, hyperelastic constitutive models, and a finite-range repulsive contact energy. Nonlinear equilibrium is solved using a regularized, matrix-free Newton-Krylov method with two-level preconditioning. Automatic differentiation evaluates tangent-vector products without forming or storing the primary tangent matrix, while GPU execution parallelizes element and quadrature-point computations. Constitutive, shell, contact, and self-contact responses were assessed against analytical, semi-analytical, and published benchmarks. At a contact-free plate equilibrium, implicit sensitivities of the converged apex displacement to constitutive parameters, thickness, and pressure agreed with finite differences from independent nonlinear simulations. Simulations of three patient-specific aortic-valve models (two tricuspid and one bicuspid) achieved final relative equilibrium residuals below 10^-4. Median GPU runtimes were approximately 15-25 minutes, with 5.3-6.5-fold speedups relative to corresponding CPU runs on the tested hardware. These results provide component-level verification and demonstrate GPU-accelerated forward valve simulation in the tested cases, supporting future gradient-based inverse studies.

infographic.key_insight: A differentiable JAX finite-element solver combines large-deformation shells and contact to simulate patient-specific aortic valves with 5.3–6.5× GPU speedups over corresponding CPU runs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster valve mechanics simulations could support assessment of tissue properties and geometry, with future potential for gradient-based parameter identification and intervention planning.
method: Energy-based finite-strain extensible-director shells with hyperelastic materials and finite-range repulsive contact.
Regularized matrix-free Newton–Krylov equilibrium solver with two-level preconditioning.
Automatic differentiation for tangent-vector products and GPU-parallel element and quadrature computations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Component benchmarks and contact-free plate sensitivity checks supported verification; three patient-specific valves reached relative equilibrium residuals below 10^-4 with median GPU runtimes of approximately 15–25 minutes.
infographic.watch_item: Sensitivity agreement was demonstrated only for a contact-free plate, leaving gradient reliability under evolving valve contact unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: A Differentiable, GPU-Accelerated Finite-Element Formulation in JAX for Large-Deformation Shells with Contact: Application to Patient-Specific Aortic Valve Simulation

title: Total Deformation-based MPM for Perfectly Elastic Solid Simulation with Strong Deformations
authors: Timna Böttcher, Rick Ridder, Jan Bender
abstract: We present a new MPM-based solver for perfectly elastic solids, which can recover from strong deformations and naturally allows contact handling. Typical MPM solvers suffer from numerical fracture, where objects break apart even when no plasticity is included in the elasticity model. Previous approaches for perfectly elastic solids solve this by computing forces on a fixed grid in the reference configuration. However, this makes them incompatible with standard collision handling methods. We instead propose a method for deformable solid simulation without numerical fracture, that still computes elastic forces on the current grid. Our method can easily include grid-based collision handling, as commonly used in MPM frameworks. Additionally, we compute the deformation directly from the particle positions and a fixed reference grid, without any updates based on velocity gradients. This facilitates the inclusion of particle-level collision handling and zero-energy mode suppression, which counteracts artifacts from non-linear deformations. As a result, we can efficiently simulate complex scenarios of elastic objects undergoing large deformations, including contact.

infographic.key_insight: Total deformation-based MPM targets numerical fracture in perfectly elastic solids while retaining current-grid force computation for contact handling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports simulation of elastic components undergoing large, recoverable deformations and contact.
method: Compute deformation directly from particle positions using a fixed reference grid, rather than velocity-gradient updates.
Compute elastic forces on the current grid to support standard grid-based collision handling.
Enable particle-level collision handling and zero-energy mode suppression to counter nonlinear deformation artifacts.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports efficient simulation of complex large-deformation elastic contact scenarios, but provides no quantitative benchmarks or error metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness and computational cost across contact conditions and discretization resolutions require validation beyond the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Total Deformation-based MPM for Perfectly Elastic Solid Simulation with Strong Deformations

title: A minimizing-movement framework for parametric finite element approximation of anisotropic curve shortening flows
authors: Wei Jiang, Chunmei Su, Ganghui Zhang
abstract: We propose a minimizing-movement framework for constructing parametric finite element methods (PFEMs) for anisotropic curve shortening flows. The cornerstone is an admissible modified energy: a smooth, convex, and iteration-dependent surrogate that majorizes the original anisotropic energy and agrees with it at the current iterate. For any fixed finite element degree $n\geq1$ and any positive surface energy density $γ\in C^2(\mathbb{S}^1)$, the unconstrained one-step problem has a unique solution for any time-step size whenever the parametric derivative of the current discrete curve does not vanish on any mesh element. It also satisfies a one-step discrete energy dissipation inequality. It therefore preserves the variational structure of the underlying $L^2$-gradient flow. The framework recovers a variational interpretation of Dziuk's isotropic scheme and applies directly to the weak anisotropies. For strong anisotropies, a convex splitting removes the weak-anisotropy restriction on the original density. A scalar constraint further extends the framework to area-preserving flows. Numerical experiments exhibit approximately the expected convergence for smooth isotropic and weakly anisotropic examples. They also confirm energy dissipation and area preservation. In the strongly anisotropic regime, the computations produce sharp facet-like profiles but reveal mesh-scale oscillations under the grid refinement.

infographic.key_insight: A minimizing-movement framework uses a smooth, convex energy surrogate to construct parametric finite element schemes with one-step energy dissipation for anisotropic curve shortening.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports variationally consistent simulation of anisotropic interface evolution, including area-preserving flows and facet-like geometries.
method: Majorize the anisotropic energy with an iteration-dependent convex surrogate that matches it at the current curve.
Solve a uniquely solvable unconstrained step for any time-step size, assuming nonvanishing elementwise parametric derivatives.
Use convex splitting for strong anisotropy and a scalar constraint for area preservation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests show approximately expected convergence for smooth isotropic and weakly anisotropic cases, energy dissipation, and area preservation.
infographic.watch_item: Strongly anisotropic tests develop mesh-scale oscillations under refinement despite producing sharp facet-like profiles.
infographic.paper_title: A minimizing-movement framework for parametric finite element approximation of anisotropic curve shortening flows

title: Convergence analysis of an augmented dual-mixed fnite element method with skew-symmetric Nitsche stabilization for the generalized Oseen equations with mixed boundary conditions
authors: Cristian Cárcamo, Abner Haguit Poza, Ramiro James Rebolledo
abstract: In this paper, we propose and analyze a new skew-symmetric Nitsche-augmented mixed scheme for the generalized Oseen equations with non-solenoidal convective fields, subject to mixed boundary conditions. The scheme is based on a continuous pseudostress-velocity augmented dual-mixed finite element formulation, in which the Dirichlet datum is imposed naturally, whereas the prescribed normal trace of the pseudostress is incorporated into the $H(div,)$ stress space. We establish the well-posedness of the continuous formulation by means of a classical lifting argument and its corresponding homogeneous problem. The essential boundary condition is then weakly enforced in the discrete scheme through suitable stabilizing Nitsche terms. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the discrete scheme, allowing the use of general conforming approximation spaces for both the pseudostress and the velocity. Moreover, in the case of homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and general Neumann data, we establish the stability of the Nitsche scheme. Under mild regularity assumptions on the exact solution, we prove optimal convergence rates in an energy norm. Finally, numerical experiments in two and three dimensions confirm the theoretical convergence rates and assess the performance of the proposed scheme for non-solenoidal convective fields and solutions exhibiting boundary layers.

infographic.key_insight: A skew-symmetric Nitsche-augmented dual-mixed finite element scheme achieves optimal energy-norm convergence for generalized Oseen equations with mixed boundary conditions and non-solenoidal convection.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports reliable finite element simulation of linearized viscous flow with mixed boundary data and boundary-layer behavior.
method: Use an augmented pseudostress–velocity dual-mixed formulation.
Weakly enforce the prescribed pseudostress normal trace using skew-symmetric Nitsche stabilization.
Prove continuous and discrete well-posedness for general conforming approximation spaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two- and three-dimensional numerical experiments confirm theoretical convergence rates and assess non-solenoidal convection and boundary-layer solutions.
infographic.watch_item: Optimal convergence requires solution regularity, and the stated stability result assumes homogeneous Dirichlet conditions with general Neumann data.
infographic.paper_title: Convergence analysis of an augmented dual-mixed fnite element method with skew-symmetric Nitsche stabilization for the generalized Oseen equations with mixed boundary conditions

title: Constrained neural softening functions for the Mullins effect in parameter-dependent materials
authors: Dominik K. Klein, Jonas Fey, Maximilian Kannapinn, Oliver Weeger
abstract: Accurately capturing the Mullins effect across varying material compositions remains challenging, as constitutive models must unify flexible representations of stress softening with physical consistency and robust parameter calibration. In this work, we investigate parameter-dependent physics-augmented neural network constitutive models within the pseudo-elastic modeling framework, focusing on structural constraints that ensure physically admissible neural softening functions. This paper has three key contributions: (1) We formulate different neural softening functions within the pseudo-elastic framework, including a multiplicative decomposition of the softening function that enables parameter-dependent ansatz functions satisfying common mechanical constitutive conditions by construction. (2) We derive a sufficient condition for ellipticity of pseudo-elastic constitutive models, which can be enforced in the constitutive models by construction. (3) We systematically investigate how flexibility and structural constraints influence the performance of neural softening functions in terms of prediction accuracy and calibration robustness. For this, we consider multiaxial experimental data of carbon black-filled EPDM rubber synthesized with varying amounts of curatives. The findings of our work suggest that neural softening functions are a promising extension of the classical pseudo-elastic framework and, when subject to suitable constraints, can improve predictive accuracy for highly nonlinear, parameter-dependent materials.

infographic.key_insight: Structurally constrained neural softening functions extend pseudo-elastic Mullins models to capture composition-dependent stress softening while preserving physical admissibility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports more accurate constitutive modeling of filled rubber across formulations, with constraints designed to improve calibration robustness.
method: Embed parameter-dependent, physics-augmented neural softening functions in a pseudo-elastic framework.
Use a multiplicative softening decomposition to satisfy common constitutive conditions by construction.
Derive an enforceable sufficient condition for ellipticity and compare flexibility–constraint trade-offs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation uses multiaxial experimental data from carbon black-filled EPDM rubber with varying curative amounts to assess prediction accuracy and calibration robustness.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the tested EPDM formulations and loading conditions remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Constrained neural softening functions for the Mullins effect in parameter-dependent materials

title: A Transfer Principle for Elliptic Carleman Estimates: Application to Discrete Calderón Stability
authors: Qi Lü, Yu Wang
abstract: We develop a transfer principle that lifts continuous elliptic Carleman estimates to mesh-uniform estimates for conforming Galerkin discretizations. The main difficulties are twofold: discrete states generally lack the \(H^2\)-regularity required by the continuous estimate, and the Carleman parameter \(s\) must be controlled relative to the mesh size \(h\). We overcome both by introducing a shifted continuous problem whose Galerkin solution is exactly the conforming reconstruction of a prescribed discrete state. Weighted approximation then transfers the inequality back to the original discrete operator without adding stabilization, and yields the range \(s\le ch^{-4/5}\) for radial weights. We verify the framework for piecewise affine finite elements with consistent or lumped mass on fitted, uniformly shape-regular meshes, and for standard Cartesian finite differences through their finite-element realization. As an application, we study the discrete Calderón problem for bounded complex Schrödinger potentials in dimension \(d\ge3\). Assuming agreement in a fixed connected boundary neighborhood and uniform stability of the discrete Dirichlet problems, we obtain stability from Dirichlet inputs and variational flux observations on independently prescribed, possibly disjoint boundary patches. The resulting estimate in \(H^{-r}\), \(r>d/2\), retains the single logarithmic data term and the \(O(h^{1/2})\) mesh remainder of the full-data estimate.

infographic.key_insight: A transfer principle converts continuous elliptic Carleman estimates into mesh-uniform estimates for conforming Galerkin discretizations without added stabilization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports stability analysis for finite-element and finite-difference inverse boundary problems, helping quantify how measurement error and mesh resolution affect potential recovery.
method: Introduce a shifted continuous problem whose Galerkin solution reconstructs the prescribed discrete state.
Use weighted approximation to transfer estimates to the discrete operator.
For radial weights, control the Carleman parameter by s ≤ c h^(-4/5).
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical verification for piecewise affine finite elements with consistent or lumped mass and Cartesian finite differences, plus partial-boundary Calderón stability with a single logarithmic data term and an O(h^(1/2)) mesh remainder.
infographic.watch_item: The inverse stability result requires d ≥ 3, potentials agreeing near the boundary, and uniformly stable discrete Dirichlet problems; no numerical benchmark is reported in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A Transfer Principle for Elliptic Carleman Estimates: Application to Discrete Calderón Stability

title: Resisting Drying Stress in Laponite Bentonite Clay Composites, Two Step Yielding and Crack Peel Selection
authors: Tapati Dutta, Agnishikha Chakrabarti, Soham Mitra, Deepshikha Das, Indranil Chakraborty
abstract: Clay films that dry on a rigid substrate crack, peel or stay intact, and which of these happens matters for coatings, barrier layers and ceramic processing. Composites of clay with polymers have been studied widely. Clay composites, whose components differ in size and charge, are much less explored. We show that mixing the nano scale clay Laponite with the micron scale clay Bentonite reduces desiccation damage on both a hydrophobic and a hydrophilic substrate, Laponite films stay essentially intact, Bentonite films fracture extensively, and on glass most intermediate compositions are less damaged than a simple average of the two would suggest. Rheology of the gelled suspensions reveals a two step yielding in every composition, and the cohesive energy derived from it depends by orders of magnitude on which step is used, a point that any rheology cracking correlation must specify. A dimensionless cohesion adhesion index, whose sign we derive from an energy balance, is consistent with compositions that peel on polypropylene and crack on glass. Replicate experiments were performed for robustness of results. The results identify composition as a simple handle on the crack resistance of clay films and open the search for the critical crack-free thickness as a function of clay composition.

infographic.key_insight: Mixing nanoscale Laponite with microscale Bentonite reduces drying damage, with most intermediate compositions on glass outperforming a simple average of the pure-clay outcomes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Clay composition offers a practical route to improve crack resistance in coatings, barrier layers and ceramic processing.
method: Compared drying damage across clay compositions on hydrophobic polypropylene and hydrophilic glass.
Measured two-step yielding in gelled suspensions and derived cohesive energies.
Used an energy-balance-based cohesion–adhesion index to interpret peeling versus cracking.
infographic.evidence_signal: Replicate experiments supported essentially intact Laponite films, extensively fractured Bentonite films and reduced damage in mixtures; every composition exhibited two-step yielding.
infographic.watch_item: Rheology–cracking correlations must specify the yielding step used because derived cohesive energies differ by orders of magnitude.
infographic.paper_title: Resisting Drying Stress in Laponite Bentonite Clay Composites, Two Step Yielding and Crack Peel Selection

title: A hyper-reduction strategy for elastoplastic hydro-mechanical problems in partially saturated soil
authors: Alba Muixí, Lluís Monforte, Antonio Rodríguez-Ferran, Sergio Zlotnik
abstract: This work proposes a hyper-reduced order model for coupled hydro-mechanical simulations of elastoplastic deformation and water flow in partially saturated soils. These simulations are used to monitor and assess the safety of geotechnical structures such as earthfill dams, where calibration, uncertainty quantification and scenario analysis require solving the same transient model many times for different parameter values. The displacement and the pore pressure are approximated in a field-split reduced basis obtained by proper orthogonal decomposition, and the Galerkin-projected equations are integrated with decomposed cubature rules, one per balance equation, built with the energy-conserving sampling and weighting (ECSW) method. Each residual is split into an affine part and a nonlinear correction: the affine part is computed exactly, at negligible online cost, so that the cubature rule only needs to approximate the correction, which is localized in space. The construction is independent of the constitutive model choices and is implemented in FEniCSx by assembling the original variational forms on the small set of elements selected by ECSW. The method is tested on two- and three-dimensional dams retaining tailings and water, simulating a raise of the dam and the subsequent consolidation phase, with the friction angle, stiffness and hydraulic conductivity of the dam material and the height of the raise as varying parameters. The hyper-reduced model reproduces the displacement and pressure fields with errors below $0.5\%$ with respect to the finite element solution, achieving speed-ups of up to $43\times$ in two dimensions and $77\times$ in three. These performance gains grow with the extent of the plastic yielding, and the selected elements concentrate in the plastified and unsaturated zones, whose size is set by the physics rather than by the mesh resolution.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-localized hyper-reduction accelerates coupled elastoplastic soil deformation and water-flow simulations while preserving displacement and pore-pressure accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster repeated simulations can support calibration, uncertainty quantification and safety assessment of earthfill dams.
method: Build separate displacement and pore-pressure reduced bases using proper orthogonal decomposition.
Evaluate affine residual terms exactly and approximate nonlinear corrections with equation-specific ECSW cubature rules.
Assemble the original variational forms only on selected elements in FEniCSx.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on 2D and 3D dams undergoing raising and consolidation reported field errors below 0.5% relative to finite elements, with speed-ups up to 43× and 77×, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy beyond the tested parameter ranges and loading scenarios remains unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A hyper-reduction strategy for elastoplastic hydro-mechanical problems in partially saturated soil

title: Non-Volatile Memory Devices for Neuromorphic Computing
authors: Debasis Das
abstract: This chapter explores the critical role of emerging non-volatile memory (eNVM) devices in advancing neuromorphic computing. Inspired by the human brain's remarkable ability to perform complex tasks like pattern recognition and adaptation, neuromorphic computing offers immense potential for implementing complex neural networks (NNs) in real hardware. Despite ongoing research into the brain's complexities, its fundamental operation relies on neurons (processing units communicating via electrochemical signals) and synapses (junctions between neurons). The modifiable strength of the synapse is key to learning and memory functionality, allowing the brain to adapt and rewire itself. For dense and low-power circuits in neuromorphic computing, these eNVM devices are ideal due to their synaptic-like behavior and non-volatile information storage. Properties such as conductance modulation of these devices emulate synaptic plasticity, which is crucial for learning, and their scalability makes them promising for large-scale neuromorphic architectures. This chapter will delve into the various types of eNVM devices such as resistive RAM (ReRAM), phase-change memory (PCM), spintronics-based memory devices, and their applications in neuromorphic computing, discussing their challenges and opportunities, and highlighting recent advances in their integration within neuromorphic systems.

infographic.key_insight: Emerging non-volatile memory devices can emulate synaptic plasticity through conductance modulation, supporting hardware neural networks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These devices offer a route to dense, low-power neuromorphic circuits with persistent synaptic weights.
method: Review ReRAM, phase-change memory, and spintronics-based memory devices.
Relate conductance modulation to biological synaptic plasticity.
Discuss neuromorphic integration advances, challenges, and opportunities.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a review chapter and reports no quantitative benchmarks or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Device scalability and synaptic-like behavior do not alone establish reliable large-scale system integration.
infographic.paper_title: Non-Volatile Memory Devices for Neuromorphic Computing

title: Optimal AFEM convergence for any bulk parameter smaller than one
authors: Lars Diening, Johannes Storn
abstract: We prove rate-optimal convergence of the standard adaptive finite element method with conforming Lagrange elements for the Poisson problem for Dörfler marking with any bulk parameter $θ\in (0,1)$. This removes the smallness restriction on the bulk parameter that has persisted in the classical theory of optimal adaptive finite element methods.

infographic.key_insight: Standard adaptive FEM achieves rate-optimal convergence for the Poisson problem with any Dörfler bulk parameter θ ∈ (0,1), removing the classical smallness restriction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result broadens theoretically justified marking-parameter choices for adaptive Poisson solvers used in engineering simulation.
method: Standard adaptive finite element method
Conforming Lagrange finite elements
Dörfler marking with any θ ∈ (0,1)
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical convergence proof, not numerical benchmarks or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: The stated guarantee concerns the Poisson problem and does not establish equivalent results for general solid-mechanics models or learned surrogates.
